title: Waking
hookLine: many Christians make their first thought a prayer, before the phone
tomorrow: can you give away a day before you've seen it?

lines: THE WHOLE TOWN AT THE DOOR.
SO WHY SLIP OUT BEFORE DAWN?
cards: The alarm goes off, and the phone is right there, and so is everything in it: the news, the group chat, the inbox. Here's an odd detail in Mark's Gospel.
The night before, the whole town of Capernaum crowded at the door where Jesus was staying. He was the one everybody wanted.

And in the morning, “rising up a great while before day,” he slips out to a solitary place to pray. When Simon tracks him down, he says, “All men seek for thee.” So why leave the people who were looking for him?

teach.h: LET US GO INTO THE NEXT TOWNS.
teach.b: Read one more line and the puzzle solves itself. Jesus answers Simon: “Let us go into the next towns, that I may preach there also.” He doesn't go back to the crowd at the door.
Something in that early hour set the direction of the day before anyone else's wants could. The first voice he listened to wasn't the town's. The Psalms had already put the morning first.

teach.h: MY VOICE SHALT THOU HEAR IN THE MORNING.
teach.b: Psalm five: “My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up.” Direct, like aiming. Look up, like waiting for an answer.

teach.h: WHEN I AWAKE, I AM STILL WITH THEE.
teach.b: Psalm one hundred thirty-nine gives the gentlest version: “when I awake, I am still with thee.” Not I'd better start talking to God now, but God was already there while I slept.
Christians have built small habits on lines like these. Some say a verse before standing up. Some make the sign of the cross.
Some just say thank you. The words matter less than the order.
The first thought goes to God; the phone, the news and the worry still come, they just don't get to speak first.
One to tell a friend tonight: in Mark, the dawn prayer is what sends Jesus somewhere new, not back to where he was wanted.

how: Some Christians begin the day with a short prayer, a psalm verse or the sign of the cross before getting out of bed and before reaching for the phone.

giving the first minute of the day to God

morning prayer means a long routine before the day can start
the habit is the order: the first thought to God, even one line or a thank you.
Psalm 139 says when I awake, I am still with thee
God was there first, while the sleeper slept.

games.q: your group chat blew up overnight: drama, dozens unread. you've just woken up. what does Mark's morning suggest?
o: catch up fast, so nothing gets worse while you pray.
a first word to God, then open the chat.
stay off the chat all day, to keep the morning holy.
games.why: Jesus didn't ignore people; he went on to the next towns. but the first hour went to prayer, and it set the direction.

practice: Sit the way you do when you've just woken, with your phone face down and out of reach.
Let your hands rest open, and choose the first words you'll give tomorrow morning before the screen: perhaps when I awake, I am still with thee, or a plain thank you.

wordCard.voice: Waking. The first minute of the day, given to God before the phone, the news or the worry.

orig.note: Hebrew for morning, the word Psalm 5 repeats.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: first thought, God, and everything else gets the second. See you in the morning.
